name: Gandhi
era: 1869 to 1948, and a living example since
line: Hold to the truth, harm no one and do your own work with your hands.

quote.text: I have nothing new to teach the world. Truth and non-violence are as old as the hills.

quotes.text: Non-violence is the greatest force at the disposal of mankind.
Recall the face of the poorest and the weakest man whom you may have seen, and ask yourself if the step you contemplate is going to be of any use to him.
quotes.source: A note known as the Talisman, written in August 1947; printed in Pyarelal, Mahatma Gandhi: The Last Phase, 1958

quotes.text: I object to violence because when it appears to do good, the good is only temporary; the evil it does is permanent.
If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change.
quotes.source: Indian Opinion, 1913; Collected Works, volume 13. The likely source of the saying about being the change

quotes.text: Earth provides enough to satisfy every man’s needs, but not every man’s greed.
quotes.source: As reported by his secretary Pyarelal in Mahatma Gandhi: The Last Phase, 1958
Written in Bengali for a journalist who asked for a message, 1947, as commonly reported

words.usage: From sat, that which is. For Gandhi truth is not only accurate speech. It is reality itself, and he came to say that Truth is God.
Refusing to injure any living being in thought, word or deed. Gandhi made it active: the positive force of love.
The word coined in South Africa in 1908 for his method of non-violent resistance. Also translated truth-force or soul-force.
Someone who breaks an unjust law openly, accepts the penalty and bears no hatred towards the opponent.
Independence for India, and beneath that the rule of each person over their own self.
Using what is made near by, and serving one’s immediate neighbours first.
His title for his Gujarati version of Ruskin’s Unto This Last. The good of each is contained in the good of all.
Beginning with the person who has least.
Also khaddar. He called it the livery of freedom and asked every Indian to wear it in place of mill cloth.
He spun every day and put the wheel at the centre of the national flag of the 1920s.
A weighted stick for spinning by hand. Small enough to use while walking or in a meeting.
He founded four: Phoenix and Tolstoy Farm in South Africa, Sabarmati and Sevagram in India.
A promise that binds whatever one’s mood. The ashram lived by eleven of them.

words.meaning: Chastity; conduct that leads to God
words.usage: Control of all the senses. He took a vow of celibacy in 1906, at thirty-six.
Owning nothing one does not need. At his death his belongings fitted on a small tray.
He extended it: to keep more than you need while others lack is a kind of theft.
The first requirement of non-violence. He said cowardice and ahimsa do not go together.
Everyone should do some manual work for their keep, whatever else they do. An idea he took from Tolstoy and Ruskin.
Work done for others without thought of return. He called it the surest way to find oneself.
Taking suffering on oneself in place of inflicting it, in order to move an opponent’s heart.
Literally dwelling near. He fasted for self-purification and, seventeen times, as a public appeal.
He kept every Monday as a day of silence and communicated by scribbled notes.
Morning and evening prayer in the open air, with verses and hymns from several religions, was the fixed frame of his day.
Repeating a name of God. A nurse taught it to him as a child to cure his fear of the dark.
Shops shut and work ceases for a day as mourning or protest. He called one across India in April 1919.
What those close to him, and then the country, called him.
A title that attached to him from about 1915. He disliked it and said it had often pained him.
His scheme of schooling through a craft, with head, heart and hands taught together.
His picture of free India as a republic of self-sufficient villages.
One of the eleven vows. His prayer meetings read from the Gita, the Quran, the Bible and others.

practices.name: Prayer before dawn
practices.instructions: Rise before the sun and wash. Sit outside or at an open window, on the floor if you can. Keep silence for five minutes. Then read aloud a short passage from the scripture or poetry that means most to you, and one from a tradition that is not yours. End with a verse of a song, or a single word of peace. No belief is required; the point is to begin the day quiet and truthful. The rule of this Onda is to tell the truth.
practices.why: Gandhi’s ashram day began with a multi-faith prayer at 4:20 in the morning, in which hymns and readings from many religions were shared. A quiet start gave him the steadiness he needed.
variations: Read a poem from a different tradition.
Sing one verse of a hymn.
Sit outside in the cold light.

practices.name: Half an hour of handwork
practices.instructions: Spend thirty minutes making or mending something useful with your hands: spin, knit, sew a seam, darn, weave, carve, repair a tool. Sit upright, work steadily and do not listen to anything. Let the rhythm of the work hold your attention. The rule of this Onda is to do some work with your hands each day.
practices.why: Gandhi spun cotton daily and asked everyone in the movement to do the same, as a way to share in physical work and to dignify it. Handwork steadies the mind.
variations: Sharpen a knife or fix a hinge.

practices.name: A brisk morning walk
practices.instructions: Walk briskly for half an hour at the start of the day, in the open air. Gandhi walked in the morning and evening for decades and could keep pace with men half his age. Swing your arms and breathe deeply. Greet whoever you meet. Walk at a pace that suits your health.
practices.why: Gandhi was a tireless walker and believed walking was the best exercise. A daily walk was a part of every day at the ashram.
variations: Walk barefoot on a safe path.
Walk with a friend and talk of one question.
Walk to a place you usually drive to.

practices.name: One fearless act
practices.instructions: Choose one thing today that you have been afraid to do, and do it, with truth and without harm to anyone. Abhaya, fearlessness, was the first of Gandhi’s qualities of a good person. Say the hard thing kindly, ask for the thing you want, or stand in line for what is fair. The rule of this Onda is to fear nothing.
practices.why: Gandhi said that fearlessness is the first requisite of spirituality. A small fearless act each day builds it like a muscle.
variations: Phone someone you have been avoiding.
Say no when you mean no.

practices.name: Use something local
practices.instructions: Today, choose to use or buy something made close to home by people you could meet: bread from a local baker, vegetables from a neighbour, cloth from a nearby maker. Swadeshi is the principle of preferring what is made nearby. Notice who made it. Thank them if you can. Even one local choice makes a small circle.
practices.why: Swadeshi, using what is made in your own country and community, was a core part of Gandhi’s programme. It ties your purchases to the people who make things.

practices.name: A plain breakfast with warm lemon water
practices.instructions: Drink a glass of warm water with lemon and a little honey when you wake, and eat a plain breakfast of fruit, nuts or dates. Eat simply and sparingly, as the ashram did. Chew slowly and finish what you take. Notice how light the morning feels. The rule of this Onda is to eat simply. Skip any food your health needs, and ask a doctor if unsure.
practices.why: Gandhi ate simple vegetarian food and experimented with diet all his life. A plain breakfast is a gentle version of his habit.
variations: Skip one extra, such as sugar or salt.
Eat in silence for five minutes.

practices.name: Clean it yourself
practices.instructions: Do the dirtiest job in your household or workplace yourself today, with care and without complaint. Clean the toilet, take out the rubbish, scrub the drain, wash everyone’s dishes. Do it thoroughly and tell nobody. While you work, think about the people who do such jobs every day for a living, and how they are treated.
practices.why: Gandhi cleaned latrines himself and insisted that every ashram member do so, to break the idea that some work is beneath anyone. It is a humbling exercise in bread labour.
variations: Clean a shared space at work.

practices.name: The talisman
practices.instructions: When you are in doubt today, or when the self becomes too much with you, stop. Call to mind the face of the poorest and weakest person you have ever seen. Ask whether the step you are considering will be of any use to them. Will it give them anything? Will it restore them to a control over their own life? If the answer is yes, go on. Doubts melt away.
practices.why: Gandhi gave this test in a note written in 1948 and called it a talisman. It is a short, searching question for any decision.
variations: Use it for a work decision.
Write the test on a card.

practices.name: Answer your letters
practices.instructions: Answer your pending letters and messages today, by hand if possible. Gandhi answered every letter that came to him, often with the left hand when the right was tired, and sometimes sat up until midnight to finish. Choose the most important three. Reply truthfully and kindly. Clear the heap.
practices.why: Gandhi wrote an extraordinary number of letters and articles, and was a faithful correspondent. Clearing your own pile is a practical act of respect.
variations: Reply to a message from a stranger.

practices.name: A non-violent no
practices.instructions: Choose one thing you disagree with today and say no to it without anger and without harm. Satyagraha, holding to truth, means refusing to cooperate with what you think wrong while treating everyone as a person. Say it clearly, give your reason and accept the consequences. Don’t shout, don’t sneer. Hold your ground gently.
practices.why: Satyagraha was Gandhi’s method of non-violent resistance, based on truth and firmness. A small daily version trains the temper and the spine.
variations: Say no to an unfair request.
Refuse to join a piece of gossip.

practices.name: Own less
practices.instructions: Choose one thing you own and do not need, and give it to someone who does. Gandhi died owning very little: his glasses, sandals, a watch, a bowl, a few books. Look around and pick one item. Wrap it, deliver it and don’t wait for thanks. The rule of this Onda is to own little.
practices.why: Aparigraha, non-possession, was one of Gandhi’s vows. Giving away one thing a day is a step towards a lighter life.
variations: Pass on a tool you rarely use.

practices.name: Another faith’s verse
practices.instructions: Read one verse or short passage from a faith that is not yours: a psalm, a sutra, a hadith, a Gita verse. Read it slowly and respectfully. Sarva dharma samabhava, equal respect for all religions, was the principle of Gandhi’s prayer meetings. Note one line that you could live by.
practices.why: Gandhi’s prayer meetings drew on all the world’s religions and were open to everyone. Reading across traditions was one of his everyday habits.
variations: Read the Sermon on the Mount.

practices.name: Evening prayer and silence
practices.instructions: At dusk walk for ten minutes, briskly, without talking. Then sit down. Go back over the day and ask where you departed from the truth: an exaggeration, a convenient silence, a promise not kept. Ask whom you harmed, in word or deed or thought. Make a plan to put right what you can. Close with a quiet verse and then silence.
practices.why: Gandhi’s evening prayer and his regular self-examination were part of every day. His great principle was to account to himself for his conduct.

practices.name: An hour of silence
practices.instructions: Keep one hour of silence this evening, as Gandhi did every Monday. Don’t speak, don’t message, don’t watch anything. Read, write, do handwork, walk. If someone needs you, communicate on paper. Notice how much of what you say is unnecessary. When the hour ends, speak your first words slowly and truly.
practices.why: Gandhi kept a day of silence every week, from which he said he drew strength and clarity. An hour is a gentle way to try it.
variations: Keep silence for the evening meal.

practices.name: A page of experiments with truth
practices.instructions: Write one page about something you did today that was an experiment with truth: a moment when you tried to tell the truth, act without harm or serve someone. Describe what happened, what you felt and what you learned. Gandhi called his autobiography the story of his experiments with truth. Keep your own record.
practices.why: Gandhi’s autobiography treats his life as a series of experiments, with honest accounts of failure. A page a night builds that honesty.

practices.name: Sing Vaishnava Jana To
practices.instructions: Play or sing Vaishnava Jana To, the 15th-century Gujarati hymn that was Gandhi’s favourite. It describes the person who feels the pain of others, helps them without pride and is free of envy. Follow a translation, and sing the refrain. It was sung at his prayer meetings every day.
practices.why: Narsinh Mehta’s hymn was Gandhi’s favourite, and describes his ideal of a good person. Singing it brings its words into the body.

practices.name: A plain supper of khichdi
practices.instructions: Cook a pot of khichdi, rice and lentils cooked soft with a little salt and perhaps a pinch of turmeric, and eat it for supper. It is a plain, nourishing, cheap dish that feeds many. Eat it slowly and finish your plate. Share a bowl with a neighbour or housemate. Simplicity can be delicious.
practices.why: Khichdi is the everyday comfort food of India and was a regular at the ashram. It is a lesson in how little a good meal needs.

practices.name: Ask forgiveness
practices.instructions: Before bed, think of someone you have hurt or let down and ask their forgiveness, in person, by message or by letter. Say plainly what you did and that you are sorry, without excuses. Gandhi urged that the strong forgive and the brave apologise. Then rest.
practices.why: Forgiveness, he said, is the attribute of the strong. Asking for it is as hard and as freeing as granting it.
variations: Forgive someone who has not asked.

practices.name: A day of quiet
practices.instructions: Keep silence for half a day. Don’t talk, text or watch. Do handwork, walk, read, cook and clean. Eat simply. Carry a notebook if you need to communicate. Tell your household the night before. Gandhi kept silence every Monday and used it to write. At the end of the morning, speak your first words slowly and truthfully.
practices.why: The day of silence, maun, was Gandhi’s weekly habit. A morning of it gives a taste of the rest it brought him.
variations: Do it with a friend in separate rooms.

practices.name: A salt march
practices.instructions: Take a long walk with a group, up to two hours, for a cause or in memory of one. In 1930 Gandhi walked 240 miles to the sea at Dandi to make salt in defiance of the British monopoly. Agree a route and a purpose, such as clearing a river bank or visiting a shelter. Walk steadily, share water and sing as you go.
practices.why: The Salt March was a masterpiece of non-violent protest. A group walk with a purpose borrows its spirit without any of its danger.
variations: Walk to a local landmark and clean it.
Walk to a food bank with donations.
Walk with a banner of kindness.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of Gandhi’s Autobiography
immersePlan.text: Read a short chapter of his story of experiments with truth. Mark a place where he admits a failing.

immersePlan.name: Read Hind Swaraj
immersePlan.text: Read a few pages of Gandhi’s 1909 pamphlet on true self-rule, written as a dialogue on a ship. Note the questions he is asked.

immersePlan.name: Read Ambedkar’s Annihilation of Caste
immersePlan.text: Read the opening of Ambedkar’s 1936 speech, a sharp challenge to Gandhi and the caste system. Think about the other side of the story.

immersePlan.name: Watch part of Gandhi
immersePlan.text: Watch the first hour of Richard Attenborough’s 1982 film, with Ben Kingsley as Gandhi. Notice the train scene in South Africa.

immersePlan.name: Watch Lage Raho Munna Bhai
immersePlan.text: Watch the 2006 comedy in which a Mumbai gangster is visited by Gandhi’s ghost and starts using Gandhigiri. It is warm and funny.

immersePlan.name: Watch the Salt March newsreel
immersePlan.text: Watch the surviving film of the 1930 march to the sea at Dandi. Notice the quiet crowds.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Vaishnava Jana To
immersePlan.text: Play M. S. Subbulakshmi’s or another singer’s version of Gandhi’s favourite hymn. Follow a translation.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Raghupati Raghava Raja Ram
immersePlan.text: Play the song that became the anthem of the Salt March, with its line Ishwar Allah tero naam. Sing the refrain.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Abide with Me
immersePlan.text: Play the Christian hymn Gandhi loved, which was sung at his ashram and played at his funeral. Sit still for the verses.

immersePlan.name: Look at Nandalal Bose’s linocut of Gandhi
immersePlan.text: Look at the bold black-and-white print of Gandhi walking with his staff, made for the Salt March. Notice how few lines it uses.

immersePlan.name: Look at Bourke-White’s photograph
immersePlan.text: Look at Margaret Bourke-White’s 1946 photograph of Gandhi reading at his charkha. Notice the light and the stillness.

immersePlan.name: Look at Gandhi’s possessions
immersePlan.text: Look at the photograph of everything he owned at his death: sandals, glasses, watch, bowl, spittoon and books. Count them.

immersePlan.name: Eat fruit, nuts and dates
immersePlan.text: Eat a plain snack of seasonal fruit, a handful of nuts and a few dates. Chew slowly.

immersePlan.name: Cook khichdi
immersePlan.text: Cook rice and lentils together until soft, with salt and a little turmeric. Eat it with yogurt and share it.

immersePlan.name: Taste jaggery
immersePlan.text: Eat a small piece of unrefined cane sugar with a cup of warm water. Compare its taste to white sugar.

immersePlan.name: Drink a cup of warm milk
immersePlan.text: Drink a cup of warm milk, goat’s if you can find it, or plant milk. Gandhi took goat’s milk daily in his later years.

immersePlan.name: Drink warm lemon water with honey
immersePlan.text: First thing in the morning, drink a glass of warm water with lemon juice and a spoon of honey.

immersePlan.name: Drink boiled and cooled water
immersePlan.text: Drink a glass of water that has been boiled and cooled. Think of those who do not have clean water.

immersePlan.name: Wear something handmade
immersePlan.text: Wear something made by hand, or made nearby, today. Khadi is the homespun cloth Gandhi urged everyone to wear. Notice the feel.

immersePlan.name: Keep an hour of silence
immersePlan.text: Keep an hour of silence today as Gandhi did on Mondays. Don’t talk, text or watch anything.

immersePlan.name: Hold a small prayer meeting
immersePlan.text: Gather one or two people for ten minutes of readings, a song and silence. Include a passage from a faith not your own.

immersePlan.name: Play football
immersePlan.text: Play football with friends or watch a game. Gandhi organised football clubs in South Africa, the Passive Resisters Soccer Club.

immersePlan.name: Try spinning with a drop spindle
immersePlan.text: Try spinning wool or cotton with a drop spindle. Time yourself and see how much you spin in ten minutes.

immersePlan.name: Play gilli-danda
immersePlan.text: Play the village game with a short stick, the gilli, struck with a longer stick, the danda. Play in an open space and mind your distance.

immersePlan.name: Mark Gandhi Jayanti
immersePlan.text: Gandhi Jayanti falls on 2 October, also the International Day of Non-Violence. Do an act of service and read a passage.

immersePlan.name: Mark the Salt March
immersePlan.text: Between 12 March and 6 April, remember the 1930 march. Walk for twenty minutes in silence for a cause you care about.

immersePlan.name: Look up Sabarmati Ashram
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the ashram on the Sabarmati river in Ahmedabad, where Gandhi lived from 1917 to 1930. Imagine the day there.

immersePlan.name: Practise satya
immersePlan.text: Satya is truth. Tell one truth today that you would normally soften.

immersePlan.name: Practise satyagraha
immersePlan.text: Satyagraha is holding to truth. Stand firm, gently, on one small matter.

immersePlan.name: Practise sarvodaya
immersePlan.text: Sarvodaya is the welfare of all. Do one thing today that benefits everyone around you, not just yourself.

rules.why: No lies, no exaggeration, no convenient silence. If you cannot say it truthfully, do not say it.
Not in act, word or thought. Oppose what a person does and keep goodwill towards the person.
Keep only what you use. What you hold beyond your need belongs to someone who lacks it.

rules.text: Do some work with your hands each day
rules.why: Make, mend, grow or clean. No task is beneath you.
Plain food, few items, nothing for the sake of the palate alone.
Not loss, not opinion, not authority. Without courage there is no non-violence.

read.title: An Autobiography: The Story of My Experiments with Truth
read.creator: M. K. Gandhi, trans. Mahadev Desai
read.why: Written in weekly instalments, mostly in prison. Frank about his failures, his diet, his marriage and how he became who he was. It stops in 1921.

read.title: Hind Swaraj
read.creator: M. K. Gandhi
read.why: Written in ten days on a ship, as a dialogue. A fierce short attack on modern civilisation and a statement of what real self-rule would be.

read.title: Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World, 1914 to 1948
read.creator: Ramachandra Guha
read.why: The fullest modern biography, drawing on archives across four continents. Admiring and critical.

read.title: Unto This Last
read.creator: John Ruskin
read.why: The book a friend gave him for a train journey in 1904. He did not sleep that night and changed his life the next morning.

read.title: The Kingdom of God Is Within You
read.creator: Leo Tolstoy
read.why: The argument for Christian non-resistance that overwhelmed him as a young lawyer.

read.title: Annihilation of Caste
read.creator: B. R. Ambedkar
read.why: The undelivered speech by his greatest Indian critic, with Gandhi’s reply and Ambedkar’s rejoinder. Essential for seeing where Gandhi fell short.

watch.title: Gandhi
watch.creator: Richard Attenborough
watch.why: The epic film with Ben Kingsley. It simplifies, but the Salt March and the funeral are staged on the scale they happened.

watch.title: The Making of the Mahatma
watch.creator: Shyam Benegal
watch.why: The twenty-one years in South Africa, where a shy lawyer became a leader. Based on a book by Fatima Meer.

watch.title: Lage Raho Munna Bhai
watch.creator: Rajkumar Hirani
watch.why: A Mumbai gangster starts seeing Gandhi and tries truth and kindness on his enemies. A hit comedy that made his methods popular with a new generation.

watch.title: Newsreels of the Salt March
watch.creator: Various cameramen
watch.why: A few minutes of silent film survive: a thin man with a staff walking very fast, and the crowd behind him.

listen.title: Vaishnava Jana To
listen.creator: Narsinh Mehta; sung by M. S. Subbulakshmi and many others
listen.why: A Gujarati hymn describing the true devotee as one who feels the pain of others. Sung at his prayer meetings daily.

listen.title: Raghupati Raghava Raja Ram
listen.creator: Traditional; as sung on the Salt March
listen.why: The chant of the marchers, with a line added to say that Ishwar and Allah are both God’s names.

listen.title: Abide with Me
listen.creator: Henry Francis Lyte and William Henry Monk
listen.why: His favourite Christian hymn. Indian military bands played it at the close of Republic Day ceremonies for decades.

listen.title: Gandhi’s voice
listen.creator: Recorded at Kingsley Hall, London
listen.why: A six-minute statement on God, the only studio recording he made. Slow, quiet and exact.

art.title: Bapuji, 12 April 1930
art.creator: Nandalal Bose
art.why: A linocut in black and white: Gandhi striding with his staff on the Salt March. The image that fixed him in the Indian mind.

art.title: Gandhi at his spinning wheel
art.creator: Margaret Bourke-White
art.why: The photograph for Life magazine, with the wheel large in the foreground. She had to learn to spin before she was allowed to take it.

art.title: Gyarah Murti
art.creator: Devi Prasad Roy Choudhury
art.why: Eleven bronze figures of every kind of Indian follow Gandhi along a road in New Delhi.

art.title: His possessions
art.creator: National Gandhi Museum, New Delhi
art.why: Spectacles, sandals, a watch, a bowl and spoon, a small book of songs. Almost everything he owned.

eat.title: Fruit, nuts and dates
eat.creator: Whatever is in season, with a few almonds or peanuts
eat.why: For years he lived mainly on raw food. He experimented with his diet all his life and wrote a book about it.

eat.title: Boiled vegetables without spices
eat.creator: With unpolished rice or a little bread
eat.why: Ashram food was plain on principle: food is to keep the body in service, not to please the tongue.

eat.title: Khichdi
eat.creator: Rice and lentils cooked soft together
eat.why: The simplest complete meal in India, and what a guest at Sevagram would be given.

eat.title: Jaggery
eat.creator: Unrefined cane sugar
eat.why: He preferred it to white sugar as a village product, and distributed it to break fasts.

drink.title: Goat’s milk
drink.creator: A cup, warm
drink.why: Having vowed never to drink cow’s or buffalo’s milk, he was persuaded by his wife during an illness that the vow did not mention goats. He took a goat with him to London in 1931.

drink.title: Warm water with lemon and honey
drink.creator: First thing in the morning
drink.why: His usual start to the day.

drink.title: Water
drink.creator: Boiled and cooled
drink.why: He took no tea, coffee or alcohol and campaigned for prohibition.

customs.title: Wearing khadi
customs.creator: Cloth you or your neighbours have spun
customs.why: From 1921 he wore only a short loincloth and shawl of homespun, so as to dress like the poorest Indian.

customs.title: The day of silence
customs.creator: Every Monday
customs.why: He would not speak from Sunday evening to Monday evening, and wrote notes on scraps of paper when necessary. He used the day to catch up on letters.

customs.title: The prayer meeting
customs.creator: Open to anyone, morning and evening
customs.why: Hymns, readings from several scriptures and a short talk. He was shot on his way to one.

customs.title: The eleven vows
customs.creator: Recited daily at the ashram
customs.why: Truth, non-violence, chastity, control of the palate, non-stealing, non-possession, fearlessness, removal of untouchability, bread labour, equal respect for religions and swadeshi.

games.title: Football
games.creator: Team sport · South Africa
games.why: He helped found football clubs in Durban, Pretoria and Johannesburg, all named the Passive Resisters, and used the matches to talk to crowds about resistance.

games.title: Spinning contests
games.creator: Ashram and Congress pastime
games.why: Who can spin the most even yarn in an hour? Competitions with the wheel and the drop spindle were held at national gatherings.

games.title: Gilli-danda
games.creator: Village game · India
games.why: A short stick is flicked into the air and struck with a longer one. It needs nothing that money can buy, which is the swadeshi of games.

festivals.title: Gandhi Jayanti
festivals.creator: 2 October
festivals.why: His birthday, a national holiday in India and the United Nations International Day of Non-Violence. Prayer meetings are held at Raj Ghat.

festivals.title: Martyrs’ Day
festivals.creator: 30 January
festivals.why: The day of his assassination in 1948. India keeps two minutes of silence at eleven in the morning.

festivals.title: Anniversary of the Salt March
festivals.creator: 12 March to 6 April
festivals.why: Groups still walk the route from Sabarmati to the sea at Dandi, some 385 kilometres.

places.title: Sabarmati Ashram
places.creator: Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India
places.why: His home from 1917 to 1930 on the bank of the river. His small room, Hriday Kunj, is kept as it was. The Salt March started from the gate.

places.title: Sevagram Ashram
places.creator: Wardha, Maharashtra, India
places.why: A cluster of mud and bamboo huts in the middle of India where he lived from 1936. Still a working community. Visitors can stay.

places.title: Gandhi Smriti
places.creator: Tees January Marg, New Delhi, India
places.why: The house where he spent his last 144 days. Concrete footprints lead across the lawn to the spot where he fell.

places.title: Raj Ghat
places.creator: New Delhi, India
places.why: A black marble platform by the Yamuna marks the place of his cremation. An eternal flame burns at one end. Remove your shoes.

places.title: Pietermaritzburg railway station
places.creator: KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
places.why: Where he was thrown off a train in June 1893 for sitting in a first-class carriage. A plaque on the platform and a small exhibition mark the night that changed him.

places.title: Mani Bhavan
places.creator: Laburnum Road, Mumbai, India
places.why: His base in Bombay for seventeen years, now a museum with his room, his wheel and a fine library.

ethics.title: Truth
ethics.text: Be truthful in thought, speech and action, and be ready to admit error publicly. He called his biggest retreat a Himalayan miscalculation, in print.
ethics.practice: Correct one thing you said today that was not quite true.

ethics.title: Non-violence
ethics.text: Refuse to injure, and go further: wish your opponent well and try to win them over.
ethics.practice: Do one kindness today for someone who has wronged you.

ethics.title: Non-possession
ethics.text: Reduce your wants. Simplicity frees you for service and frees resources for others.
ethics.practice: Give away one thing you have not used in a year.

ethics.title: Bread labour
ethics.text: Share in the manual work that keeps you alive. It breeds respect and breaks down caste and class.
ethics.practice: Do one job today that you normally pay or expect someone else to do.

ethics.title: Fearlessness
ethics.text: Truth and love require courage. He preferred violence to cowardice, and non-violence to both.
ethics.practice: Say the true thing you are afraid to say.

ethics.title: Service of the last
ethics.text: Measure any plan by what it does for the weakest.
ethics.practice: Apply the talisman to one decision today.

philosophy.title: Truth is God
philosophy.text: He began by saying God is Truth and ended by reversing it. Truth is the one thing even an atheist cannot deny. Each of us sees only a part.
philosophy.practice: Whose partial truth have you dismissed this week?

philosophy.title: Means and ends
philosophy.text: The means are the end in the making. A just society cannot come from unjust methods, any more than a rose from a weed’s seed.
philosophy.practice: Is there something good you are pursuing by a doubtful method?

philosophy.title: Satyagraha
philosophy.text: Resist injustice openly, without violence and without hatred, accepting the suffering this brings. The aim is to convert the opponent, not to defeat them.
philosophy.practice: Think of a conflict you are in. What would it look like to seek the other’s change of heart?

philosophy.title: Swaraj
philosophy.text: Political freedom is worthless without mastery of oneself. A nation of people ruled by their appetites will only change masters.
philosophy.practice: What rules you that you would like to rule?

philosophy.title: Swadeshi
philosophy.text: Our first duty is to those nearest. Buy from, work with and serve your neighbours before the distant and abstract.
philosophy.practice: Find out where one thing you used today was made, and by whom.

philosophy.title: Trusteeship
philosophy.text: Whatever wealth or talent you hold beyond your needs, you hold in trust for society.
philosophy.practice: What are you a trustee of, and for whom?

philosophy.title: Sarvodaya
philosophy.text: A good economy is one in which the last person is provided for. There can be no welfare of some at the cost of others.
philosophy.practice: Who pays the hidden cost of your comfort?

philosophy.title: The experiment
philosophy.text: He called his life experiments with truth. Every conviction was to be tested in practice, and revised if it failed.
philosophy.practice: Choose one belief and design a week’s test of it.

journal: Where did you depart from the truth today?
Whom did you harm, in word or thought?
What did you make or mend with your hands?
What do you own that you do not need?
What were you afraid of?
What work did you leave to someone else because it was beneath you?
Who was the poorest person you saw today, and did you look at them?
What did you eat for pleasure alone?
What wrong did you go along with?
Towards whom do you carry ill will?
What promise did you keep at a cost?
What did you want that you did well to refuse?
Where did your means not match your ends?
What mistake should you admit publicly?
Whom did you serve today?
What did silence show you?
Where did you exaggerate?
What in you still needs to be governed?
Whose truth did you fail to hear?
What did you buy, and who made it?
Whom do you treat as untouchable?
What would you go to prison for?
Where did anger rule you?
What did the dawn give you?
How much is enough for you?
What are you a trustee of?
Whom have you not forgiven?
What experiment is your life running now?
What would your day say, if your life were your message?
What will you hold to tomorrow?
reflect: What did strict truthfulness cost you, and give you?
What did working with your hands change?
What have you given up, and do you miss it?
Whom do you oppose without hating?
Whose face do you now call to mind when you decide?

intro: Mohandas Gandhi was born in 1869 in Porbandar, a small port on the coast of Gujarat, into a family of the merchant caste that had served as chief ministers to local princes. His mother was devout and given to long fasts. He was married at thirteen, was an indifferent student, and at eighteen was sent to London to become a barrister. He came home qualified and so shy that he could not speak in court.

In 1893 he took a year’s contract with an Indian firm in South Africa. A week after landing he was thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg for refusing to leave a first-class compartment reserved for whites. He spent the night in the cold waiting room deciding whether to go home. He stayed for twenty-one years. In that time he built a law practice, led the Indian community’s resistance to discriminatory laws, founded two rural communes, took vows of poverty and celibacy, and worked out a method he named satyagraha: holding firmly to truth. Unjust laws were to be broken openly and peacefully, and the punishment accepted without retaliation, so as to move the conscience of the opponent.

He returned to India in 1915, aged forty-five, and within five years had turned the Indian National Congress from a debating club of lawyers into a mass movement. He dressed in a loincloth of homespun cotton, travelled third class, spoke to villagers in their own languages and asked them to spin, to boycott British cloth and courts, and to lose their fear. In 1930 he walked 385 kilometres to the sea to make salt in defiance of the government monopoly, and tens of thousands followed him to prison. He was jailed for a total of more than six years.

His aims went far beyond independence. He fought the practice of untouchability, worked for friendship between Hindus and Muslims, promoted village industries and a new kind of school, and treated all of it as a single religious search. Truth, he said, was God, and non-violence the way to it. He regarded his life as a series of experiments and published his mistakes.

Independence came in August 1947 together with the partition of the country and the killing of perhaps a million people. Gandhi took no part in the celebrations. He walked through the riot districts of Bengal and fasted in Calcutta and Delhi until the leaders of the communities pledged peace. On 30 January 1948, on his way to evening prayers, he was shot dead by a Hindu nationalist who thought him too generous to Muslims.

He has critics, and they have a case. As a young man in South Africa he wrote of Africans with contempt. Dr Ambedkar, the leader of the Dalits, thought his approach to caste paternalistic and inadequate. His tests of his own celibacy in old age disturbed even his followers. This Onda takes his daily discipline of prayer, handwork, plain food, humble labour and self-examination, and the talisman he left for hard decisions, and leaves you to judge the man.
guide.origin: Gujarat in western India, by way of London and twenty-one years in South Africa
guide.era: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born in 1869 and assassinated in 1948

figures.name: Mohandas K. Gandhi
figures.bio: Lawyer, editor, organiser and seeker. He weighed about fifty kilograms, laughed a great deal and answered his own post.

figures.name: Kasturba Gandhi
figures.bio: His wife for sixty-two years. Unlettered when they married, she became a satyagrahi in her own right, was jailed several times and died a prisoner beside him.

figures.name: Shrimad Rajchandra
figures.bio: A Jain jeweller and poet in Bombay, the nearest he had to a spiritual guide. Gandhi said no one else had so impressed him.

figures.name: Leo Tolstoy
figures.bio: The Russian novelist whose late religious writings shaped him. They exchanged letters in Tolstoy’s last year, and Gandhi named a farm after him.

figures.name: Gopal Krishna Gokhale
figures.bio: The moderate Congress leader he called his political guru, who told him to spend a year in India with his ears open and his mouth shut.

figures.name: Mahadev Desai
figures.bio: His secretary, translator and diarist for twenty-five years, who died in prison with him.

figures.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
figures.bio: His chosen political heir and India’s first prime minister, who shared few of his views on machines and villages and loved him all the same.

figures.name: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
figures.bio: The Pashtun leader who raised a non-violent army of a hundred thousand Muslims on the North-West Frontier. Known as the Frontier Gandhi.

figures.name: B. R. Ambedkar
figures.bio: Jurist, architect of India’s constitution and leader of the Dalits. He clashed with Gandhi over separate electorates and regarded him as an obstacle to the ending of caste.

figures.name: Sarojini Naidu
figures.bio: Poet and Congress president who led the raid on the Dharasana salt works after his arrest. She teased him that it cost a fortune to keep him in poverty.

figures.name: Vinoba Bhave
figures.bio: The scholar he chose as the first individual satyagrahi in 1940. After 1951 he walked India asking landowners to give land to the landless.

history.detail: The youngest child of the prince’s chief minister. He is married to Kasturba in 1883, when both are thirteen.
He studies law at the Inner Temple, joins the Vegetarian Society and first reads the Bhagavad Gita, in English.
Ejected from the train. Within a year he has founded the Natal Indian Congress.
After reading Ruskin overnight he moves his newspaper and its staff to a farm near Durban, where everyone draws the same wage.
At a mass meeting in Johannesburg three thousand Indians swear to go to jail sooner than register under a new pass law.
He founds an ashram at Ahmedabad and admits an untouchable family, which nearly ends it.
His first Indian campaigns: for indigo growers in Bihar, drought-hit farmers in Gujarat and mill workers in the city.
After the massacre at Amritsar he leads a national boycott. When a mob burns policemen alive at Chauri Chaura he calls it off, and is sentenced to six years.
With seventy-eight companions he walks from Sabarmati to Dandi and picks up a lump of salt from the shore. Some sixty thousand people are arrested in the months that follow.
In prison he fasts against separate electorates for the depressed classes. Ambedkar yields under pressure and signs a compromise he always resented.
He calls on the British to leave at once and is interned in the Aga Khan Palace at Pune, where Kasturba and Mahadev Desai die.
At seventy-seven he walks barefoot from village to village in riot-torn East Bengal. On independence day he is fasting and spinning in a Muslim house in Calcutta.
Nathuram Godse fires three shots at close range in the garden of Birla House in Delhi.

concepts.text: Truth as the ground of being.
concepts.detail: More than honesty. Since no one possesses the whole truth, no one has the right to coerce another, which is why truth requires non-violence.
Not passivity. He distinguished the non-violence of the brave, which could strike and chooses not to, from that of the weak.
A method with rules: open declaration, no secrecy, no violence, no hatred, willingness to suffer and readiness to negotiate at any moment.
In Hind Swaraj he argues that India is held by Indians’ own cooperation and desires, and will be free when individuals govern themselves.
Economic self-reliance through local production, above all hand spinning. The burning of foreign cloth was its most dramatic sign.
A social order built up from the last person, with dignity of labour and equal value for all work.
The rich are to keep what they reasonably need and act as trustees of the rest. Critics thought it naive. He thought it the only alternative to class war.
Spinning, sanitation, basic education, Hindu-Muslim unity, removal of untouchability, uplift of women. He considered it more important than civil disobedience.
Undertaken to purify himself or to awaken the conscience of those who loved him. He held that one may fast only against a friend, never to coerce an enemy.

facts.text: He was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize five times and never received it. The committee later publicly regretted the omission.
He wrote with either hand, and his collected works fill a hundred volumes.
He never held any office in the government of India.
On the Salt March he walked about sixteen kilometres a day at the age of sixty-one, and younger marchers struggled to keep up.
He carried a watch pinned to his loincloth and was fanatical about punctuality.
The saying about being the change you wish to see in the world does not appear in his writings in those words.

sensitivity.note: Gandhi is revered in India as the father of the nation and is also seriously criticised there and elsewhere. This Onda borrows his daily discipline and his tests of conduct. It does not present him as a saint, and it leaves out his fasts and his more extreme experiments.
requiredCaveats: In his early years in South Africa Gandhi wrote of black Africans in demeaning terms and sought privileges for Indians apart from them. His views changed, but the record stands.
Many Dalits, following Dr Ambedkar, regard his approach to caste as patronising and reject the name Harijan that he gave them.
Long fasts are dangerous. Nothing here asks you to fast, and people with any history of disordered eating should skip the food rules.
His celibacy experiments in old age involved young women in his care and were wrong by any ordinary standard.
